intro: Between about 500 BCE and 500 CE, people on three sides of the world built states larger and more lasting than anything before. Greek city-states invented citizen government and the habit of asking why. Rome turned a hill town into an empire of sixty million people, held together by roads, law and Latin. India's emperors and China's dynasties governed tens of millions with written edicts, examinations and a shared script. Historians call these the classical worlds because later ages kept returning to them for models.

This unit follows a potter climbing to the Athenian Assembly, a baker in Pompeii on the morning Vesuvius woke, and a caravan leaving Chang'an with silk. It asks how each society decided who could rule and who was left out, how it fed and defended itself, what it believed, and what happened when it fell. It also follows the threads that tied them together: Alexander's road to India, Greek styles on Buddhist statues, Indian numbers on Roman shores, and plague on the Silk Roads.

By the end you will be able to explain where democracy, republics, juries, paper, zero, the Senate and the civil service came from, and to argue, with evidence, which classical legacy matters most in your own life in Illinois.
bigQuestion: What did the classical worlds of Greece, Rome, India and China build that we still live with, and what did those achievements cost?

timeline.t: Solon cancels debts and opens the Athenian assembly to all citizens
Romans drive out their last king and found the Republic

Alexander defeats the Persian king at Gaugamela
Ashoka renounces conquest after the Kalinga war
The king of Qin unites China as First Emperor

The last western Roman emperor is removed

test.q: Why did ancient Greece develop as many small city-states?
choices: Mountains and the sea separated communities
Each Greek god required a city
test.why: Rugged geography cut valleys and islands off from one another, so each became its own polis.

test.q: Which group in Athens could vote?
choices: Free adult men born to Athenian parents
test.why: Only free adult male citizens voted; women, foreigners and the enslaved were excluded.

test.q: What method did Socrates use to teach?
test.why: Socrates questioned people until they saw the gaps in what they thought they knew.

test.q: What happened to Greek culture after Alexander's death?
choices: It spread across a wide area and mixed with local cultures
test.why: The Hellenistic age blended Greek language and learning with Egyptian, Persian and Indian traditions.

test.q: Why did Rome have two consuls who served one year?
choices: To prevent any one man from becoming a king
To lead the eastern and western halves
Because the Twelve Tables required it
test.why: Shared, limited power was the Republic's guard against one-man rule.

test.q: What made the plebeians' demand for the Twelve Tables important?
choices: The laws were written and public for all citizens
test.why: Public written law meant priests and nobles could no longer bend secret rules.

test.q: What most weakened the Roman Republic before Caesar?
choices: Armies loyal to generals rather than the state
test.why: Landless soldiers followed whoever paid them, letting generals march on Rome.

test.q: How did Augustus keep power without being called king?
choices: He kept the Republic's forms while controlling the army and treasury
test.why: As first citizen he let the Senate meet but held the real power.

test.q: Which Roman legal idea is still used in American courts?
test.why: The presumption of innocence and the right to face one's accuser come through Roman law.

test.q: What was true of the fall of Rome in 476?
choices: The eastern empire fell the same year
Roman laws, towns and Latin continued under new rulers
test.why: Odoacer removed the last western emperor, but Roman institutions carried on, and the east lasted until 1453.

test.q: How do we know Ashoka's own thoughts?
choices: From edicts he had carved on rocks and pillars
test.why: More than thirty of Ashoka's edicts survive in his own words.

test.q: Which is an achievement of Gupta India?
test.why: Indian mathematicians developed place-value numbers with zero during the Gupta age.

test.q: What did the Han dynasty take from Confucius?
choices: The idea that just rulers and dutiful officials create order
The belief that people must be ruled by fear
The design of the terracotta army
test.why: The Han made Confucian learning official and trained officials in it.

test.q: Why did silk cost far more in Rome than in China?
choices: It passed through many traders who each took a profit
test.why: No merchant went the whole way; goods changed hands many times, each with a markup.

test.q: Which statement best sums up the Silk Roads?
choices: One road built by Rome to China
A route used only for silk
A network that carried goods, ideas and diseases across Eurasia
test.why: The Silk Roads were many land and sea routes that spread trade, religions, inventions and plague.

write.prompt: Which classical legacy matters most in your life today: Athenian democracy, Roman law and government, Indian numbers and religion, or Chinese paper and the civil service? Make a claim, support it with at least three pieces of evidence from the unit, and explain your reasoning.
tips: State your claim in one clear sentence: name the legacy and say it matters most.
Use specific evidence: a date, a person, an invention or a rule from the lessons, such as juries, zero, paper or consuls.
Explain your reasoning: show how each piece of evidence connects to something you actually do or rely on.
Address the other side: name one rival legacy and explain why yours matters more.
Be honest about cost: mention who was excluded or who paid for the achievement you chose.
